title: Black History Month: Cannabis, Prohibition and Equity

body:
For Black History Month, cannabis history deserves a clear-eyed look. For generations, cannabis laws and the way they were enforced fell especially hard on Black Americans, from the jazz era to drug-war arrest records. Today's legal market, Michigan's included, grew out of that history. Here's the documented story, plus practical ways to support Black-owned cannabis businesses all year.

## Why Black History Month, cannabis history and equity belong together

Black History Month started small. Historian Carter G. Woodson announced Negro History Week in February 1926, and the observance grew into a full month that was nationally recognized in 1976, according to the National Archives. The idea was simple: Black Americans' history should be studied, not skipped.

Cannabis belongs in that conversation because the plant's legal story is tangled up with race. Many of the musicians who shaped early cannabis culture were Black. Prohibition-era propaganda singled out jazz musicians. And Black Americans have been arrested under marijuana laws at far higher rates than white Americans. Who gets to build a business in today's legal market is part of the same story.

As a Michigan dispensary, we think that history is worth telling straight. This article follows the long arc. For profiles of the advocates, entrepreneurs, physicians and scientists shaping the field now, see our guide to [Black cannabis pioneers](/blog/black-cannabis-pioneers/).

| Year | What happened |
|---|---|
| 1926 | Carter G. Woodson's first Negro History Week |
| 1937 | Congress passes the Marihuana Tax Act after Harry Anslinger's campaign |
| 1970 | The Controlled Substances Act places marijuana in Schedule I |
| 1976 | Black History Month gains national recognition |
| 2018 | Black Americans are 3.64 times as likely as white Americans to be arrested for marijuana possession |
| 2018 | Michigan voters legalize adult-use cannabis |
| 2026 | A national study reviews equity programs in 17 adult-use states |

## Cannabis, jazz and Black culture in the early 1900s

Jazz grew out of Black communities in New Orleans and traveled north to Chicago, New York and beyond. By the 1920s and 1930s, cannabis moved through that world too. In jazz slang, a "viper" was someone who smoked it, and the music said so openly.

Cab Calloway sang "Reefer Man." Ella Fitzgerald sang "When I Get Low, I Get High," a 1936 number, with Chick Webb's orchestra. Violinist Stuff Smith wrote "If You're a Viper," a tune Fats Waller later recorded. These songs were playful and public, played in clubs and on records across the country.

Louis Armstrong is a well-known example. The Louis Armstrong House Museum notes that he called the plant "gage" and first tried it in Chicago. In the early 1930s he was arrested in California for smoking marijuana. The museum suggests his fame may have helped keep his time in jail to a little over a week.

That visibility mattered. Cannabis was part of a celebrated, very public Black art form, and it became easy for officials to link the two. When the federal government turned against the plant, jazz and the people who made it were right in the frame.

## How prohibition-era propaganda targeted Black musicians and communities

Harry Anslinger led the Federal Bureau of Narcotics and became a powerful voice against marijuana. U.S. Customs and Border Protection's own history notes that his campaign led to the Marihuana Tax Act of 1937. The act regulated importing, growing, possessing and selling marijuana, and a violation could bring a fine of up to $2,000, up to five years in prison, or both.

Newspapers and magazines carried the message. A 2020 review in the Journal of Cannabis Research points out that the New York Times ran only eight articles mentioning marijuana between 1851 and 1930, then 133 from 1931 to 1940. Of 17 magazine articles on marijuana published from mid-1937 to mid-1939, 10 came from Anslinger's bureau itself.

Those stories linked the plant to crime, violence, sex and immorality. The same review describes how American drug scares have cast certain groups as a "dangerous class" to justify prohibition. For cannabis, those groups included Mexican immigrants and jazz musicians, and the fears behind the campaigns were rooted in racism and xenophobia.

One caution: when you see a dramatic Anslinger quote online, look for where it was first published. The documented record, his bureau's press campaign and the 1937 law, tells the story clearly enough. Our history of [anti-cannabis propaganda](/blog/anti-cannabis-propaganda-history/) covers the films and headlines of the era in more depth.

## The War on Drugs and unequal arrests and sentencing

In 1970, the Controlled Substances Act placed marijuana in Schedule I, the strictest federal category. A year later, President Nixon called drug abuse "public enemy number one." Our [War on Drugs history](/blog/war-on-drugs-cannabis-history/) walks through the decades that followed.

The arrest numbers show who paid the price. The ACLU's 2020 report covered arrests from 2010 to 2018. In 2018, it found, a Black person was 3.64 times more likely than a white person to be arrested for marijuana possession, up from 3.31 times in 2010. That gap held even though Black and white Americans use marijuana at similar rates. In 2018 alone, the ACLU counted almost 700,000 marijuana arrests, more than 43% of all drug arrests that year.

The pattern wasn't new. An earlier ACLU report counted more than 8 million marijuana arrests nationwide from 2001 to 2010. It found Black Americans 3.73 times as likely as white Americans to be arrested for possession.

Sentencing laws raised the stakes. Mandatory minimum sentences became a core part of federal drug law in the 1980s. They tie prison time to the type and amount of a drug, which leaves judges less room to weigh the person in front of them.

A record also lasts. A marijuana conviction can surface in background checks for jobs and apartments long after a case closes. Families feel it too, through lost income and time apart. That lasting damage is why clearing old records is now a central part of the equity conversation.

## Legalization and the push for equity: a short bridge

States began legalizing cannabis for adults in the 2010s. Michigan voters joined them in 2018, and the state's adult-use law took effect on December 6 of that year. As legal stores opened, many advocates argued that the new market should include the communities that had borne the brunt of enforcement. That idea is usually called social equity.

Why do equity programs exist at all? Opening a licensed cannabis business is expensive and complicated. Real estate, security systems, testing, compliance staff and license fees add up long before the first sale. People with less access to money, or with an old marijuana record, faced the steepest climb, even though their communities had carried the heaviest enforcement.

A 2026 study by George Washington University researchers reviewed the 17 adult-use states that had equity programs for cannabis entrepreneurs as of May 2025, Michigan among them. Every program required equity applicants to hold majority ownership of the business. Most also offered training, financial help or reduced fees.

Results so far are uneven. In states that reported the data, minority-held licenses ranged from 11.3% of all licenses in Vermont to 60.3% in New Jersey. The authors suggested these programs may need more time to mature before their full effect shows. Our explainer on [cannabis social equity](/blog/cannabis-social-equity/) covers how equity programs work, including Michigan's.

## Michigan today: where to learn about social equity licensing and clearing records

Michigan's Cannabis Regulatory Agency licenses the state's adult-use and medical cannabis businesses. If you're curious about equity licensing, start with the social equity explainer linked above, then check the agency's current program terms before you plan around them. Programs and fees change, so go straight to the regulator for the latest.

Clearing old records is the other half of the work. Legal sales going forward don't erase convictions from before, so some people still carry old marijuana cases. Our guide to [Michigan marijuana expungement](/blog/michigan-marijuana-expungement/) explains who may qualify, how the process works and where to find free help.

For the wider legal picture, from purchase limits to where you can consume, see our [Michigan cannabis laws guide](/cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/). A few practical steps:

- **If you have an old conviction,** read the expungement guide first, then talk with a legal aid office or a lawyer about your own case.
- **If you're thinking about a cannabis business,** look at the state's current equity terms and talk with an advisor before you commit money.
- **If you want to help someone else,** share accurate information. A record that could be cleared does no good sitting untouched.

## Ways to support Black-owned cannabis businesses and advocacy groups all year

Black History Month is a good start, not a finish line. To keep the support going in every season:

- **Ask who makes it.** Every Michigan cannabis label names the producer and its state license number. Our budtenders are happy to help you look into a brand.
- **Look past the logo.** A brand's own website usually says who founded it. Founders and current ownership aren't always the same, so it's fair to ask.
- **Back record-clearing.** Legal aid groups and clinics that help people clear old convictions often rely on volunteers and donations.
- **Choose established groups.** Before you give to an advocacy organization, check that it's active and that its work matches what it says.
- **Buy legal.** Licensed stores are part of the regulated, tax-paying market that equity programs were built around.

Adults 21 and older can shop at High Society's eight Michigan stores, and registered medical patients 18 and older can too. Thank you for taking this history seriously. Please consume responsibly.

faq.q: How did the War on Drugs affect Black communities?
faq.a: Unequally and for a long time. Black Americans were arrested for marijuana far more often than white Americans, even though both groups use it at similar rates. Those arrests could mean jail time, lost jobs, housing barriers and a record that followed people for years. Mandatory minimum sentences raised the stakes further. Equity programs and record-clearing efforts are attempts to repair some of that damage.

faq.q: Are Black Americans arrested for marijuana more often than white Americans?
faq.a: Yes. The ACLU found that in 2018 a Black person was 3.64 times more likely than a white person to be arrested for marijuana possession, and the gap had not narrowed since 2010. That gap existed even though Black and white Americans use marijuana at similar rates. Clearing the records those arrests left behind is now a big part of equity work in Michigan and other states.

faq.q: What is a cannabis social equity program?
faq.a: It's a state effort to help people from communities hit hardest by marijuana enforcement take part in the legal industry. Programs often offer reduced licensing fees, training or financial help, and many require equity applicants to hold majority ownership. A 2026 study counted 17 adult-use states with programs for entrepreneurs, including Michigan. Eligibility and benefits vary by state and change over time.

faq.q: Can old marijuana convictions be cleared in Michigan?
faq.a: Possibly. It depends on the conviction and the rest of your record, and the process has its own steps. Start with our guide to Michigan marijuana expungement, which explains who may qualify and where to find free help. Then talk with a legal aid office or a lawyer about your own case before you file anything.

faq.q: How can I support Black-owned cannabis brands?
faq.a: Start by asking. Check the producer named on the label, read the brand's own background and ask who founded and owns it today. Then keep it going after February: share the brands you like with friends 21 and older, support groups that help clear old convictions and buy from licensed stores. Our budtenders are happy to help you look into a brand.

claims.claim: Carter G. Woodson announced Negro History Week in February 1926; Black History Month was nationally recognized in 1976.
claims.evidence: Opened 2026-10-24: Woodson "sent out a press release announcing Negro History Week in February, 1926"; "Fifty years after its start, Black History Month was nationally recognized in 1976."

claims.claim: Takeaway: "Federal marijuana prohibition arrived with the Marihuana Tax Act of 1937".
claims.fix: The cited CBP history describes a law that taxed and regulated marijuana (in principle stopping recreational use), not a formal ban. Reworded: the act "brought marijuana under federal control".
claims.evidence: "the Marihuana Tax Act of 1937, under which the importation, cultivation, possession and/or distribution of marijuana were regulated"; "In principle, the Marihuana Tax Act of 1937 stopped only the use of the plant as a recreational drug."

claims.claim: Harry Anslinger led the Federal Bureau of Narcotics and his campaign led to the Marihuana Tax Act of 1937, which regulated importing, growing, possessing and selling marijuana.
claims.evidence: "Federal Bureau of Narcotics Commissioner Harry Anslinger became a powerful anti-marijuana voice. His campaign against Cannabis led to the passage of the Marihuana Tax Act of 1937".

claims.claim: A violation of the 1937 act "could bring a $2,000 fine, five years in prison or both".
claims.fix: These are maximums. Reworded to "a fine of up to $2,000, up to five years in prison, or both".
claims.evidence: "Violation of the act resulted in a fine of not more than $2,000 and/or imprisonment for up to five years."

claims.claim: ACLU: "from 2010 to 2018" a Black person was "on average 3.64 times" more likely than a white person to be arrested for marijuana possession (takeaway, timeline table, body, FAQ).
claims.fix: 3.64 is the 2018 rate ratio, not a 2010-2018 average (2010 was 3.31). Takeaway, table row, body and FAQ now say "in 2018"; the body now says the 2020 report covered 2010 to 2018 and that the 2018 ratio was "up from 3.31 times in 2010" and the FAQ says the gap had not narrowed since 2010.
claims.evidence: Report PDF (linked from the ACLU publication page), Table 6 "Black and White Marijuana Possession Rates (2010-2018)": 2010 ratio 3.31 ... 2018 ratio 3.64; text: "in 2010, Black people were 3.31 times more likely ... and in 2018, they were 3.64 times more likely -- the greatest disparity of the past nine years."

claims.claim: The arrest gap exists even though Black and white Americans use marijuana at similar rates.
claims.evidence: "even though Black and white people use marijuana at similar rates".

claims.claim: In 2018 the ACLU counted almost 700,000 marijuana arrests, more than 43% of all drug arrests.
claims.evidence: "In 2018 alone, there were almost 700,000 marijuana arrests, which accounted for more than 43 percent of all drug arrests."

claims.claim: An earlier ACLU report counted more than 8 million marijuana arrests from 2001 to 2010 and found Black Americans 3.73 times as likely to be arrested for possession.
claims.evidence: June 3, 2013: "Between 2001 and 2010, there were over 8 million pot arrests in the U.S."; "Blacks are 3.73 times as likely to be arrested for marijuana possession."

claims.claim: The New York Times ran 8 articles mentioning marijuana from 1851 to 1930 and 133 from 1931 to 1940 (2020 Journal of Cannabis Research review).
claims.evidence: Full text read via Europe PMC (fullTextXML): "from 1851 to 1930, only 8 articles with 'marijuana' or 'marihuana' appeared in the New York Times. In the next decade alone (1931-1940), this number jumped to 133 articles".

claims.claim: Of 17 magazine articles on marijuana from mid-1937 to mid-1939, 10 came from Anslinger's bureau.
claims.evidence: "From July 1937 to June 1939, 17 magazine articles were published on marihuana, 10 of which were produced by the Federal Bureau of Narcotics."

claims.claim: Propaganda linked marijuana to crime, violence, sex and immorality; drug scares cast groups (Mexican immigrants, jazz musicians) as a "dangerous class"; the fears were rooted in racism and xenophobia.
claims.evidence: "sensationally linked marijuana to crime, violence, sexuality, and immorality"; "Mexican immigrants, jazz musicians, countercultural youth, and AIDS patients ... served as a 'dangerous class'"; "social fears rooted in racism, xenophobia, classism, ageism".

claims.claim: Louis Armstrong called the plant "gage" and first tried it in Chicago.
claims.evidence: "Gage as he affectionately referred to the plant"; "It was actually in Chicago when I first picked up my first stick of gage".

claims.claim: Armstrong was arrested in California in the early 1930s and "His fame helped keep his time in jail to a little over a week."
claims.fix: The museum hedges. Reworded: "The museum suggests his fame may have helped keep his time in jail to a little over a week." Arrest timing (early 1930s) kept.
claims.evidence: "in March of 1931, Louis was arrested in California for smoking marijuana. Although his celebrity may have helped him to spend only a little over a week in jail".

claims.claim: "Viper" was jazz slang for a cannabis smoker; Cab Calloway sang "Reefer Man"; violinist Stuff Smith wrote "If You're a Viper", later recorded by Fats Waller.
claims.evidence: Fats Waller, "If You're a Viper" (1943): "a cover of this Stuff Smith composition" and "a loving ode to the viper subculture of jazz musicians who revere the cannabis plant"; Cab Calloway, "Reefer Man" (1933 film International House).

claims.claim: Ella Fitzgerald recorded "When I Get Low, I Get High" in 1936.
claims.fix: WBGO dates the song (written 1936) and pairs Ella with Chick Webb's orchestra; the recording-date entry (UCSB Discography of American Historical Recordings) returned 403 to both fetch routes, so the recording year was not opened. Reworded: Ella "sang 'When I Get Low, I Get High,' a 1936 number, with Chick Webb's orchestra."
claims.evidence: "Ella Fitzgerald 'When I Get Low, I Get High' Written in 1936 by drummer and bandleader Chick Webb ... Between the rich sound of Webb's Orchestra and ... Ella".

claims.claim: In 1970 the Controlled Substances Act placed marijuana in Schedule I, the strictest federal category.
claims.evidence: Full text: "When Congress enacted the CSA in 1970, it placed marijuana in schedule I."

claims.claim: In 1971 President Nixon called drug abuse "public enemy number one".
claims.evidence: June 17, 1971: "America's public enemy number one in the United States is drug abuse."

claims.claim: Mandatory minimum sentences became a core part of federal drug law in the 1980s and tie prison time to drug type and amount.
claims.evidence: Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986 "created the basic framework of mandatory minimum penalties currently applicable to federal drug trafficking offenses" ... "based on the type and amount of drug mixture involved in the offense".

claims.claim: States began legalizing cannabis for adults in the 2010s.
claims.evidence: "In 2012, Colorado and Washington became the first States to legalize the nonmedical use of marijuana."

claims.claim: Michigan voters legalized adult use in 2018; the law took effect December 6, 2018.
claims.evidence: "Initiated Law 1 of 2018, effective Dec. 6, 2018"; "the 2018 voter law".

claims.claim: A 2026 study by George Washington University researchers reviewed the 17 adult-use states with equity programs for cannabis entrepreneurs as of May 2025, Michigan among them; every program required majority ownership; most offered training, financial help or reduced fees; minority-held licenses ranged from 11.3% (Vermont) to 60.3% (New Jersey); programs may need more time to mature.
claims.evidence: Abstract via NCBI E-utilities: J Public Health Manag Pract 2026;32(3), Epub 2026 Jan 9, GWU affiliations; "17 states with non-medical cannabis retail (as of May 2025)"; "Each state required majority ownership"; "training n = 14, financial n = 12, reduced fees n = 10"; "Massachusetts/Michigan: 100%"; "minority-held licenses (Vermont: 11.3% to New Jersey: 60.3%)"; "allow greater time for SE initiatives to mature".

claims.claim: Intro: "For most of the last century, cannabis laws and the way they were enforced fell hardest on Black Americans, from 1920s jazz halls..."
claims.fix: "Hardest" ranks groups the sources do not rank, and Armstrong's museum notes the plant was not yet illegal when he first used it in 1927. Reworded: "For generations, ... fell especially hard on Black Americans, from the jazz era to drug-war arrest records."
claims.evidence: ACLU arrest-disparity findings; Reid 2020 names Mexican immigrants alongside jazz musicians; LAHM: "When Armstrong first used marijuana ... it wasn't illegal."

claims.claim: "The people most often arrested under drug laws were very often Black Americans."
claims.fix: The ACLU data compare arrest rates, not absolute counts. Reworded: "Black Americans have been arrested under marijuana laws at far higher rates than white Americans." The sentence was split into three short ones.
claims.evidence: "Black people are 3.64 times more likely than white people to be arrested for marijuana possession".

claims.claim: Michigan's Cannabis Regulatory Agency licenses adult-use and medical cannabis businesses.
claims.evidence: "licenses and regulates adult-use and medical marijuana businesses".

claims.claim: Every Michigan cannabis label names the producer and its state license number.
claims.evidence: "name and license number of the producer (and packager)".

claims.claim: Equity programs often offer reduced fees, training or financial help, and many require majority ownership (FAQ).
claims.evidence: "Each state required majority ownership"; "Most provided support (training n = 14, financial n = 12, reduced fees n = 10)".

claims.claim: High Society: eight Michigan stores; adults 21+; medical card holders 18+; budtenders help customers with products.
claims.evidence: "Recreational shopping is available to individuals 21 years or older."; "Individuals 18 and older with a medical marijuana card can also make purchases."; staff "trained and knowledgeable".

review.notes: Writer's note kept: Michigan set-aside and equity-program details are left to the sibling articles (michigan-marijuana-expungement, cannabis-social-equity); no staff stories, donations or partnerships; no named brands or groups. Fact-check 2026-10-24: 27 claims checked, 7 fixed (ACLU 3.64 ratio was the 2018 figure, not a 2010-2018 average; 1937 act penalties are maximums; 1937 act regulated rather than banned; Armstrong jail-time cause hedged as the museum hedges it; Ella recording year not opened, reworded; two overstated framing sentences softened). Sources list unchanged (6, all opened and supporting).
